description: Somos un equipo con habilidades de desarrollo e interés en el espacio, la IA y la educación. Proponemos Misión Luna: un juego para administrar una base lunar durante siete días, gestionar recursos y resolver emergencias con ayuda de un tutor de IA. Buscamos personas con interés en programación, diseño, investigación científica y comunicación. ¡Únete para aprender, aportar ideas y crear una experiencia educativa juntos!
summary:
Survival Mars is a free, bilingual, 3D isometric browser game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge and designed for children ages 7 to 12. Set on the NE Syrtis plateau of Mars (a finalist landing site for the Mars 2020 mission), it challenges players to command a 10- or 15-sol scientific mission by managing a habitat, greenhouse, laboratory, solar arrays and communications.

Each sol, players split a limited power budget between life support, oxygen, food and research while keeping battery reserves for the next day. They send crew members, each wearing a personal dosimeter, on spacewalks to collect water ice, Martian rocks and regolith, while watching suit oxygen and radiation exposure. With the regolith, players build the habitat's radiation shield section by section.

Emergencies such as dust storms, micrometeorites and solar flares must be solved in seconds, and advice from Earth arrives late because of the communication delay. Solar flare risk is based on NASA DONKI data (a recent query when online, or a labelled historical archive), and every consequence cites its NASA source. No choice is free: kids learn real mission trade-offs through simplified, clearly labelled game rules grounded in NASA data.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Survival Mars is a free 3D game that runs in any web browser, with no install and no account. Kids aged 7 to 12 command a base on the NE Syrtis plateau on Mars (one of the three finalist landing sites for Mars 2020) for 10 or 15 sols. Each sol they split a limited power budget between life support, the greenhouse, communications and the science lab. They choose which of four astronauts goes on a spacewalk (each one wears a personal dosimeter), collect regolith, water ice and Martian rocks in a 4-slot backpack while suit oxygen drains, and spend the regolith to build the habitat's radiation shield section by section: the roof blocks more solar flare radiation, and the walls block more of the daily background radiation. Emergencies such as dust storms, solar flares and micrometeorites must be solved in seconds, and advice from Earth arrives late because of the communication delay. No choice is free.

What benefits does it have?

It turns real NASA data into decisions a child can experience, and it explains terms like sol, millisievert or solar conjunction right when they matter. Every consequence cites its NASA source, and the game clearly separates live data, stored data and simplified game rules. It runs on slow school computers (light graphics mode) and on phones, in English and Spanish, with voice narration, two difficulty levels (Cadet and Commander), a tutorial and a guided building mission. Progress is saved automatically, and there is a guide for teachers.

What is the expected impact?

Students learn to reason about real mission trade-offs (power versus science, exploring versus staying safe from radiation) and to explain them in their own words instead of memorizing facts. Because it is free and open source, any school can use it in class with no cost or sign-up, and teachers in other countries can adapt it.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

JavaScript (native modules, no buir the 3D world, HTML and CSS, NASAOpen APIs (DONKI), automated tests in Node.js (30+ tests and thousands of simulated games to balance the difficulty), GitHub, and Cloudflare Pages for hosting. The video was produced with Python, Playwright, a neural text-to-speech voice and ffmpeg. We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code and Codex); the team designed the game, reviewed and tested every change, and verified the data against the cited NASA source

How is your project creative?

Radiation is a decision, not just a number on the screen: who goes outside (each astronaut accumulates their own dose), how long they stay out, and which shield section to build first. When NASA DONKI reports a strong solar flare, the game reacts, even in the middle of a spacewalk. Everything happens in an isometrictrolled by keyboard or a touchjoystick.

What factors did your team consider?

Plain language that a 7-year-old can follow, with explanations at the moment they are needed; accessibility (voice narration, two languages, phones and slow computers); scientific honesty (stored data is never presented asre labelled); privacy (no accounts,progress stays in the player's bronstead of punishing; and a balancewith no "safe" option: playing passively survives with only 1 star, and reckless choices end badly.
